The U.S. military wants a record $1.5 trillion for the next fiscal year --
$440 billion more than it got last year.

But there's a Pentagon-sized problem: it can't tell you what happened to the
taxpayer money it already has.

This week, the Pentagon
[admitted](https://comptroller.war.gov/Portals/45/Documents/afr/fy2026/DoW_FY26_Agency_Financial_Report.pdf)
revealed it failed its annual audit for the ninth year in a row. It has never
passed one since it first tried in 2018.

But don't worry! Passing an audit is on their to-do list, says Secretary of
War Pete Hegseth.

No other major federal department has a record like this. Even the Department
of Homeland Security, which failed its first eight audits, has passed every
year for more than a decade.

If you were expecting someone to lose their job over this, think again. No
Pentagon comptroller has ever been fired over a failed audit. In fact, the man
who oversaw this one as acting comptroller just got the job permanently,
courtesy of the Senate.

And if you thought the Pentagon might at least be embarrassed, wrong again.
Its [press
release](https://www.war.gov/News/Releases/Release/Article/4649444/new-dow-
audit-progress-marks-breakthrough-toward-a-department-wide-clean-opinion/)
spins the whole thing a "breakthrough."

War Secretary Pete Hegseth took a victory lap too, declaring his department
"more than halfway there." Halfway, that is, to something literally every
other department in the government has passed for years.

It's like a restaurant that's failed nine straight health inspections putting
out a press release celebrating a breakthrough: _NOW WITH FEWER RATS!_

Even the progress is a magic trick. On paper, the list of "material
weaknesses" (auditor-speak for "your books are a mess") shrank this year, from
26 to 14. Sounds like progress, right?

Nope!

As the Inspector General's audit chief, Brett Mansfield, put it: "Although the
number of material weaknesses appears lower in FY 2026, those reductions stem
from consolidation, not resolution." In other words, the Pentagon got its 26
unpaid parking tickets down to 14 by stapling them together.

The fix, per the press release, is "Super Intelligence," the Trump
administration's Marvel-style term for Artificial Intelligence. Per the
release:

> "Today, the Department of War (DoW) released the Fiscal Year (FY) 2026
> Agency Financial Report, reflecting a new centralized approach in financial
> management and employing Super Intelligence (SI) to end wasteful processes
> and solve financial vulnerabilities."

The Pentagon has been throwing tech money at this problem for years. Back in
2021, it [hired](https://www.nextgov.com/artificial-
intelligence/2025/08/pentagon-cuts-set-back-critical-ai-data-platform/407578/)
Booz Allen Hamilton for $674 million to build an accounting tool. This year it
gave Accenture up to $821 million to overhaul that tool, and it says it has
put another $200 million into "Super Intelligence."

A lot of good that did!

Rep. Rashida Tlaib is one of only a handful of members of Congress who has
even mentioned this insane scandal. "The Pentagon FAILED its NINTH audit in a
row. Now, they demand a record $1.5 trillion while gutting Medicare, Medicaid,
SNAP, and Social Security," she said on X.

By my count, only six members of Congress have even remarked on the failed
audit. And not a single one of the newly elected members have said a word.

Congress has formally given the Pentagon until the end of 2028 to pass.
Hegseth swears they'll make it. I'll put a bet on the fact that they won't --
that is, without changing the terms and swapping out new standards for old
ones.

In the meantime, we hardly even speak about let alone debate what the
Pentagon's $1.5 trillion budget request goes towards.

For a sense of scale, look at Wall Street this week. Anthropic, the AI company
behind Claude, just went public in what the AP calls the biggest IPO ever on
record. Investors priced the value of the entire company at $1.5 trillion.
That's one year's worth of profit for the military.

We know why the country's biggest agency gets away with passing an audit. But
what happened to Congress questioning the overall defense budget? If you add
in the budget of homeland security, intelligence, and the Veterans
Administration, the national security budget is nearly double that, at $2.1
trillion.

I cannot find virtually any post-election calls by members of Congress to
reduce overall defense spending. Only Tlaib and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed
comes close, the latter saying on election-night that taxes should be spent on
domestic needs instead of funding war.

Failed audit or not, absent a public uproar, that's not likely to happen. So
how about some uproar?
